ann_85.text: Through this part, an international plan clearly raises the typical customer's predicted chance of leaving from about 1% to about 20%.
Customer-service calls (0 to 3) slightly raise it from about 1% to about 4%, and a higher night-time charge slightly raises it to about 2%.

More daytime minutes (112 to 249) slightly lower it from about 2% to about 1%, more evening minutes and a voice-mail plan slightly lower it, and more international minutes, a higher evening charge, more night-time minutes, a longer account and area code 510 slightly raise it (on the training data only).

California slightly raises it to about 5%, Washington to about 4%, Montana to about 3% and Massachusetts, Louisiana, New York, Maryland, Minnesota, Kentucky, Arizona and Oregon to about 1% to 2%, while Hawaii, New Jersey, Vermont and Illinois slightly lower it to below 1% and nine other states to about 1% (on the training data only).

ann_86.text: Through this part, customer-service calls slightly add to the predicted chance of leaving from 4 calls upwards: for the typical customer, going from 0 to 4 calls moves it from about 1% to about 3%.

For a typical customer with 3 customer-service calls (one in Idaho), a daytime charge above about 26.35 US dollars slightly lowers it, from about 5% to about 3%, and a higher evening charge also slightly lowers it (on the training data only).
Being in Alaska or Ohio slightly raises it and being in Iowa or Texas slightly lowers it, all staying at about 1% (on the training data only).

ann_87.text: Through this part, the daytime charge clearly adds to the predicted chance of leaving only once it rises above about 32.38 US dollars: for the typical customer, going from 0 to 46.09 US dollars moves it from about 1% to about 33%.
A higher daytime charge (19.07 to 42.40 US dollars) clearly raises it from about 1% to about 17% if the customer has no voice-mail messages, but not for customers with some, who stay at about 1%.
This part acts on 1390 of 4000 customers, 305 of whom left; for the typical one (a customer in Alabama with about 219 daytime minutes) it slightly raises the chance from below 1% to about 3%.
For a typical customer in Alabama with about 218 daytime minutes, voice-mail messages slightly lower it only while they stay below about 8 messages, from about 3% to below 1%.
Customer-service calls (0 to 3) slightly lower it through this part (on the training data only).

ann_88.text: This part acts on 1030 of 4000 customers, 288 of whom left, and clearly raises the typical one's predicted chance of leaving (a customer in Alabama with about 234 daytime and 236 evening minutes) from about 4% to about 13%.
Daytime minutes slightly add to it only once they rise above about 222 minutes, from about 1% to about 6% for the typical customer.
A higher evening charge slightly raises it, and even more so for customers with over 180 daytime minutes: from about 1% to about 4%, against about 1% to about 2%.
Across the usual range, more daytime minutes and a higher evening charge slightly raise it to about 2% to 3%.
For the typical customer this part acts on, being in North Carolina slightly lowers it from about 13% to about 9%, and being in Maryland slightly raises it to about 15% (on the training data only).

For a typical customer in New Hampshire, the evening charge slightly adds to it only once it rises above about 21.83 US dollars, from about 2% to about 4% (the model has little data on this: 13 customers there are past that point).

ann_89.text: Through this part, the daytime charge slightly lowers the predicted chance of leaving once it rises above about 23.13 US dollars, from about 2% to about 1% for the typical customer (on the training data only).
This part acts on 3149 of 4000 customers, 454 of whom left; for the typical one (with about 194 daytime minutes) it slightly lowers the chance from about 3% to about 2% (on the training data only).
Being in Alaska slightly lowers it to below 1% and being in New Hampshire slightly raises it to about 2% (on the training data only).

ann_90.text: Through this part, customer-service calls (0 to 3) slightly lower the predicted chance of leaving from about 2% to about 1% (on the training data only).

ann_91.text: Through this part, being in New Jersey raises the typical customer's predicted chance of leaving from about 1% to about 14% (on the training data only).
Through the linear part, New Jersey instead slightly lowers it to below 1%, and across the whole model it slightly raises it to about 3% (on the training data only).
South Carolina and Indiana slightly raise it to about 2%, while Vermont and Wyoming slightly lower it to about 1% or below (on the training data only).

ann_92.text: Across the whole model, an international plan clearly raises the typical customer's predicted chance of leaving from about 1% to about 20%.

Being in California rather than one of the states the model does not single out slightly raises it to about 5%, Washington to about 4%, Montana and New Jersey to about 3% and eleven other states to about 1% to 2%, while Vermont, Hawaii, Alaska and Illinois slightly lower it to below 1% and eleven other states to about 1% (on the training data only).
Higher evening and night-time charges slightly raise it to about 2%, and more voice-mail messages slightly lower it, staying at about 1%.

More international minutes slightly raise it to about 2%, and more night-time minutes, a longer account and area code 510 slightly raise it, while more evening minutes and a voice-mail plan slightly lower it, all staying at about 1% (on the training data only).
It ignores daytime calls, evening calls, international calls, the international charge and night-time calls.

ann_85.original: Sparse linear backbone: 35 inputs summed at identity node lin_agg (read out by the output with weight 1). Largest z-scored weights: internationalPlan +0.86 (+2.94 logit for plan holders), numberCustomerServiceCalls +0.84 (about +0.64 logit per call), totalDayMinutes -0.48 (a negative slope that the day-usage hinges override above about 200 minutes), totalNightCharge +0.21, totalIntlMinutes +0.18, voiceMailPlan -0.14, accountLength +0.10. totalEveCharge (+0.15) and totalEveMinutes (-0.12) are the same column after z-scoring, net +0.03. 24 state one-hots enter directly; their z-scored value in-state is about 7-10, so small weights become large per-state offsets: state:11 -2.35 logit (73 rows, 3 churners), state:4 +1.42 (41 rows), state:47 +1.15, state:14 -1.02, state:26 +0.90, state:46 -1.29 (plus -1.14 via unit 10379), state:31 -2.0 (cancelled by unit 2016). Note: after z-scoring, totalDayCharge and totalDayMinutes are identical columns (charge is an exact multiple of minutes), as are totalEveCharge and totalEveMinutes, so the network uses them interchangeably. Evidence (train, 4000 rows): closed form is exactly linear (closed-form error 0.006 from rounding); sensitivity summary confirms constant slopes. Its logit contribution has SD 1.42, the largest of any child.
ann_85.proposed: A linear backbone in which an international plan raises the chance of leaving from about 1% to 20% and customer-service calls slightly raise it; usage and state effects are slight.

ann_86.original: Many customer-service calls AND low day usage -> churn. 7689 = relu(0.85*CSC + 0.30); 15054 = relu(1.11*dayCharge + 1.09*state:43 + 1.09); 4397 = relu(0.78*15054 - 0.74*state:0 - 0.81*state:35 - 0.52) is a day-charge ramp; 997 = relu(0.20*CSC + 0.23*7689 - 0.49*4397 - 0.41) fires when service calls are high and day charge low. 9974 = 1.05*997 + 0.066 is always on, so the output sees about 4.81*997: 0 for 0-2 calls, +0.45 logit at 3 calls with under 160 day minutes, +1.9 at 4 calls, +3.5 at 5 and +5 at 6+ (train churn for 4+ calls and under 160 minutes is 80-100%, vs 7-34% above 200 minutes). Rare-state switches inside the gate: state:43 (95 rows) adds +9.4 to 15054 and switches the rule off entirely (up to -2.4 logit on affected rows); state:0 and state:35 subtract about 6-7 from 4397 and switch the day-usage brake off, so in those states service calls alone trigger it (up to +2.0 logit). 5728 = relu(0.99*state:6 + 0.11*997 + 0.64) is always on; 827 = relu(1.06*state:12 + 0.30*eveCharge - 1.60*5728 - 0.75) is on only in state:12 (55 rows) and with readout -0.018 gives about -0.13 logit there; state:6 has no net effect. Note: after z-scoring, totalDayCharge and totalDayMinutes are identical columns (charge is an exact multiple of minutes), as are totalEveCharge and totalEveMinutes, so the network uses them interchangeably. Evidence (train): closed form attached; local table of mean contribution by calls x day-minutes bin attached. Linearising this child (least squares on its 8 entry inputs, R2 0.39) lowers train AUC 0.910 -> 0.899; restoring it alone onto the fully linearised model raises AUC 0.834 -> 0.872.
ann_86.proposed: A customer-service step from 4 calls upwards, slightly weakened by a daytime charge above about 26.35 US dollars; all effects slight.

ann_87.original: 2899 = relu(0.72*dayCharge - 0.88*vmailMessages - 0.25*CSC - 0.55), readout +3.00: high day charge raises churn, but only for customers with no voicemail messages, and a little less for customers who call service (these are covered by the service-call units). For no-voicemail customers the mean contribution is +0.44 logit at 180-200 day minutes, +1.95 at 220-250, +3.41 at 250-300 and +5.44 above 300 (train churn 21%, 55%, 95%); for voicemail users it is about 0 below 300 minutes. Note: after z-scoring, totalDayCharge and totalDayMinutes are identical columns (charge is an exact multiple of minutes), as are totalEveCharge and totalEveMinutes, so the network uses them interchangeably. Evidence (train): closed form and local table attached. Largest single nonlinear source: linearised (R2 0.58) AUC 0.910 -> 0.897; mean-ablated -> 0.848; restored alone onto the linearised model 0.834 -> 0.888. Largely redundant with heavy_day_eve_usage (both are high-day-usage hinges).
ann_87.proposed: Daytime charge without voice-mail: above about 32.38 US dollars the charge raises the chance of leaving steeply (about 1% to 33%), but only for customers with no voice-mail messages.

ann_88.original: 1694 = relu(1.09*dayMinutes + 0.78*eveCharge + 0.02*state:20 - 0.04*state:27 - 0.85), readout +1.60: a hinge on combined day+evening usage. Zero unless day and evening usage are both well above average; mean contribution +0.55 at 200-250 day and 200-250 evening minutes, +2.05 at 250-300/200-250, +4.7 when both are above 250/300 (train churn 63-83% in those cells). The state:20 (+0.37 at most) and state:27 (-0.43 at most) weights are small per-state shifts of the threshold. Note: after z-scoring, totalDayCharge and totalDayMinutes are identical columns (charge is an exact multiple of minutes), as are totalEveCharge and totalEveMinutes, so the network uses them interchangeably. Evidence (train): closed form and day x evening table attached. Linearised (R2 0.50) AUC 0.910 -> 0.902; restored alone onto the linearised model 0.834 -> 0.872. Overlaps with day_charge_no_voicemail.
ann_88.proposed: Heavy daytime and evening usage: acting on 1030 customers, it raises a typical such customer's chance of leaving from about 4% to 13%; daytime minutes add from about 222 minutes, and the evening charge counts more above 180 daytime minutes.

ann_89.original: 6792 = relu(0.98*state:30 - 1.63*dayCharge - 0.17) is a falling ramp in day charge; 4785 = relu(0.70*state:0 - 0.81*state:30 - 1.13*6792 + 1.14), readout -0.24. Outside states 0 and 30 this is a small saturating step: 0 below about 130 day minutes, -0.27 logit above about 180 minutes (it slightly offsets the day-usage hinges). In state:0 (56 rows) 4785 rises to about 7 and gives -1.6 logit; in state:30 (74 rows) it is always 0 (+0.2 relative). Note: after z-scoring, totalDayCharge and totalDayMinutes are identical columns (charge is an exact multiple of minutes), as are totalEveCharge and totalEveMinutes, so the network uses them interchangeably. Evidence (train): closed form and table attached. Linearising it does not lower AUC (0.9107 vs 0.9102); restoring it alone adds 0.005. Mainly a state:0 offset plus a small step.
ann_89.proposed: A small daytime-charge step that slightly lowers the chance of leaving above about 23.13 US dollars, with slight Alaska and New Hampshire adjustments, on the training data only.

ann_90.original: Two single-input units on customer-service calls. 3237 = relu(-0.67*CSC - 0.64) is on only for customers with 0 calls (readout +1.09, value 0.21: +0.23 logit); 4279 = relu(0.28*CSC + 0.83) is always on, so with readout -0.25 it is linear, -0.054 logit per call. Together they bend the backbone's +0.64-per-call CSC slope slightly: 0 calls get +0.23 logit relative to a straight line. Any function of a discrete input with few values is a lookup table; this one is nearly linear. Evidence (train): closed form and table attached. Linear fit R2 0.80; linearising changes AUC by -0.0003; restoring alone adds 0.002. Nearly negligible.
ann_90.proposed: A small customer-service term that slightly lowers the chance of leaving as calls go from 0 to 3, on the training data only.

ann_91.original: Hidden units fed only by state one-hots. The categories are mutually exclusive, so the block is exactly a per-state logit offset table. 2016 = relu(1.69 - 1.61*state:31) is on outside state 31 and off inside it; with readout -1.31 it gives state:31 +2.47 logit, which cancels most of the backbone's direct state:31 term (-2.0): net +0.76 (90 rows). 10379 = relu(0.92*state:46 - 1.53*state:0 - 0.35*state:22 - 0.94) is on only in state:46: -1.14 logit there (net with backbone -2.43, 80 rows, 5 churners). 11068 (state:50, -0.39), 15556 (state:15, +0.27) and 16346 (state:40, +0.38) are single-state offsets. state:0 and state:22 only push 10379 further below zero (no effect). Evidence (train): closed form attached; linear least-squares fit on the one-hots is exact (R2 1.0), so it is functionally linear. Mean-ablating it lowers train AUC 0.910 -> 0.903: a 0.007 train-AUC gain from per-state offsets on 55-90 rows each, likely overfit (the warranted offsets from observed churn rates are about half the fitted ones).
ann_91.proposed: Per-state adjustments, chiefly a New Jersey rise to about 14% that offsets the backbone's lowering for New Jersey, on the training data only.

ann_92.original: Root: P(churn) = sigmoid(-1.258 + linear_backbone + service_calls_low_day_usage + day_charge_no_voicemail + heavy_day_eve_usage + day_charge_step_state0 + csc_zero_calls_bump + state_offsets), additive in logit; the seven children never feed each other. 25 unconnected inputs are zero-effect entries. Performance sources (train, local): full AUC 0.910; all nonlinear children replaced by least-squares linear fits 0.834 (jointly 0.833; refit L2 logistic regression 0.843). The 0.077 gain over linear comes from three hinges: day_charge_no_voicemail (restored alone +0.054, Shapley 0.031), service_calls_low_day_usage (+0.038, Shapley 0.022) and heavy_day_eve_usage (+0.038, Shapley 0.021); the two day-usage hinges overlap, so their gains are sub-additive. State one-hots act as fixed per-state offsets (direct weights and single-state units), plus three switches inside the service-call gate (state:43 off, state:0 and state:35 on).
ann_92.proposed: The model adds a linear backbone, a daytime-charge part for customers without voice-mail messages, a heavy-usage part, a customer-service part, a daytime-charge step and state adjustments; an international plan raises the chance of leaving from about 1% to 20%, and daytime calls, evening calls, international calls, international charge and night-time calls are ignored.

summary.text: For a typical customer (one in West Virginia with area code 415, an account length of 100, no international or voice-mail plan, one customer-service call and median usage such as 180 daytime minutes), the model predicts about a 1% chance that the customer leaves, and an international plan clearly raises that to about 20%.

Through one part, the daytime charge clearly adds to it only once it rises above about 32.38 US dollars: for the typical customer, going from 0 to 46.09 US dollars moves it from about 1% to about 33%.

In that part, a higher daytime charge (19.07 to 42.40 US dollars) clearly raises it from about 1% to about 17% if the customer has no voice-mail messages, but not for customers with some, who stay at about 1%.

A heavy-usage part acts on 1030 of 4000 customers, 288 of whom left, and clearly raises the typical one's chance (a customer in Alabama with about 234 daytime and 236 evening minutes) from about 4% to about 13%.

Being in California rather than one of the states the model does not single out slightly raises it to about 5%, and other states move it slightly, from below 1% to about 4% (on the training data only).
Higher evening and night-time charges slightly raise it to about 2%, and the model ignores daytime calls, evening calls, international calls, the international charge and night-time calls.

parts.name: linear_backbone
parts.original_hypothesis: Sparse linear backbone: 35 inputs summed at identity node lin_agg (read out by the output with weight 1). Largest z-scored weights: internationalPlan +0.86 (+2.94 logit for plan holders), numberCustomerServiceCalls +0.84 (about +0.64 logit per call), totalDayMinutes -0.48 (a negative slope that the day-usage hinges override above about 200 minutes), totalNightCharge +0.21, totalIntlMinutes +0.18, voiceMailPlan -0.14, accountLength +0.10. totalEveCharge (+0.15) and totalEveMinutes (-0.12) are the same column after z-scoring, net +0.03. 24 state one-hots enter directly; their z-scored value in-state is about 7-10, so small weights become large per-state offsets: state:11 -2.35 logit (73 rows, 3 churners), state:4 +1.42 (41 rows), state:47 +1.15, state:14 -1.02, state:26 +0.90, state:46 -1.29 (plus -1.14 via unit 10379), state:31 -2.0 (cancelled by unit 2016). Note: after z-scoring, totalDayCharge and totalDayMinutes are identical columns (charge is an exact multiple of minutes), as are totalEveCharge and totalEveMinutes, so the network uses them interchangeably. Evidence (train, 4000 rows): closed form is exactly linear (closed-form error 0.006 from rounding); sensitivity summary confirms constant slopes. Its logit contribution has SD 1.42, the largest of any child.
variables: number of calls to customer service

parts.name: day_charge_no_voicemail
parts.original_hypothesis: 2899 = relu(0.72*dayCharge - 0.88*vmailMessages - 0.25*CSC - 0.55), readout +3.00: high day charge raises churn, but only for customers with no voicemail messages, and a little less for customers who call service (these are covered by the service-call units). For no-voicemail customers the mean contribution is +0.44 logit at 180-200 day minutes, +1.95 at 220-250, +3.41 at 250-300 and +5.44 above 300 (train churn 21%, 55%, 95%); for voicemail users it is about 0 below 300 minutes. Note: after z-scoring, totalDayCharge and totalDayMinutes are identical columns (charge is an exact multiple of minutes), as are totalEveCharge and totalEveMinutes, so the network uses them interchangeably. Evidence (train): closed form and local table attached. Largest single nonlinear source: linearised (R2 0.58) AUC 0.910 -> 0.897; mean-ablated -> 0.848; restored alone onto the linearised model 0.834 -> 0.888. Largely redundant with heavy_day_eve_usage (both are high-day-usage hinges).
variables: number of calls to customer service

parts.name: heavy_day_eve_usage
parts.original_hypothesis: 1694 = relu(1.09*dayMinutes + 0.78*eveCharge + 0.02*state:20 - 0.04*state:27 - 0.85), readout +1.60: a hinge on combined day+evening usage. Zero unless day and evening usage are both well above average; mean contribution +0.55 at 200-250 day and 200-250 evening minutes, +2.05 at 250-300/200-250, +4.7 when both are above 250/300 (train churn 63-83% in those cells). The state:20 (+0.37 at most) and state:27 (-0.43 at most) weights are small per-state shifts of the threshold. Note: after z-scoring, totalDayCharge and totalDayMinutes are identical columns (charge is an exact multiple of minutes), as are totalEveCharge and totalEveMinutes, so the network uses them interchangeably. Evidence (train): closed form and day x evening table attached. Linearised (R2 0.50) AUC 0.910 -> 0.902; restored alone onto the linearised model 0.834 -> 0.872. Overlaps with day_charge_no_voicemail.

parts.name: service_calls_low_day_usage
parts.original_hypothesis: Many customer-service calls AND low day usage -> churn. 7689 = relu(0.85*CSC + 0.30); 15054 = relu(1.11*dayCharge + 1.09*state:43 + 1.09); 4397 = relu(0.78*15054 - 0.74*state:0 - 0.81*state:35 - 0.52) is a day-charge ramp; 997 = relu(0.20*CSC + 0.23*7689 - 0.49*4397 - 0.41) fires when service calls are high and day charge low. 9974 = 1.05*997 + 0.066 is always on, so the output sees about 4.81*997: 0 for 0-2 calls, +0.45 logit at 3 calls with under 160 day minutes, +1.9 at 4 calls, +3.5 at 5 and +5 at 6+ (train churn for 4+ calls and under 160 minutes is 80-100%, vs 7-34% above 200 minutes). Rare-state switches inside the gate: state:43 (95 rows) adds +9.4 to 15054 and switches the rule off entirely (up to -2.4 logit on affected rows); state:0 and state:35 subtract about 6-7 from 4397 and switch the day-usage brake off, so in those states service calls alone trigger it (up to +2.0 logit). 5728 = relu(0.99*state:6 + 0.11*997 + 0.64) is always on; 827 = relu(1.06*state:12 + 0.30*eveCharge - 1.60*5728 - 0.75) is on only in state:12 (55 rows) and with readout -0.018 gives about -0.13 logit there; state:6 has no net effect. Note: after z-scoring, totalDayCharge and totalDayMinutes are identical columns (charge is an exact multiple of minutes), as are totalEveCharge and totalEveMinutes, so the network uses them interchangeably. Evidence (train): closed form attached; local table of mean contribution by calls x day-minutes bin attached. Linearising this child (least squares on its 8 entry inputs, R2 0.39) lowers train AUC 0.910 -> 0.899; restoring it alone onto the fully linearised model raises AUC 0.834 -> 0.872.
variables: number of calls to customer service

parts.name: state_offsets
parts.original_hypothesis: Hidden units fed only by state one-hots. The categories are mutually exclusive, so the block is exactly a per-state logit offset table. 2016 = relu(1.69 - 1.61*state:31) is on outside state 31 and off inside it; with readout -1.31 it gives state:31 +2.47 logit, which cancels most of the backbone's direct state:31 term (-2.0): net +0.76 (90 rows). 10379 = relu(0.92*state:46 - 1.53*state:0 - 0.35*state:22 - 0.94) is on only in state:46: -1.14 logit there (net with backbone -2.43, 80 rows, 5 churners). 11068 (state:50, -0.39), 15556 (state:15, +0.27) and 16346 (state:40, +0.38) are single-state offsets. state:0 and state:22 only push 10379 further below zero (no effect). Evidence (train): closed form attached; linear least-squares fit on the one-hots is exact (R2 1.0), so it is functionally linear. Mean-ablating it lowers train AUC 0.910 -> 0.903: a 0.007 train-AUC gain from per-state offsets on 55-90 rows each, likely overfit (the warranted offsets from observed churn rates are about half the fitted ones).

parts.name: day_charge_step_state0
parts.original_hypothesis: 6792 = relu(0.98*state:30 - 1.63*dayCharge - 0.17) is a falling ramp in day charge; 4785 = relu(0.70*state:0 - 0.81*state:30 - 1.13*6792 + 1.14), readout -0.24. Outside states 0 and 30 this is a small saturating step: 0 below about 130 day minutes, -0.27 logit above about 180 minutes (it slightly offsets the day-usage hinges). In state:0 (56 rows) 4785 rises to about 7 and gives -1.6 logit; in state:30 (74 rows) it is always 0 (+0.2 relative). Note: after z-scoring, totalDayCharge and totalDayMinutes are identical columns (charge is an exact multiple of minutes), as are totalEveCharge and totalEveMinutes, so the network uses them interchangeably. Evidence (train): closed form and table attached. Linearising it does not lower AUC (0.9107 vs 0.9102); restoring it alone adds 0.005. Mainly a state:0 offset plus a small step.

parts.name: csc_zero_calls_bump
parts.original_hypothesis: Two single-input units on customer-service calls. 3237 = relu(-0.67*CSC - 0.64) is on only for customers with 0 calls (readout +1.09, value 0.21: +0.23 logit); 4279 = relu(0.28*CSC + 0.83) is always on, so with readout -0.25 it is linear, -0.054 logit per call. Together they bend the backbone's +0.64-per-call CSC slope slightly: 0 calls get +0.23 logit relative to a straight line. Any function of a discrete input with few values is a lookup table; this one is nearly linear. Evidence (train): closed form and table attached. Linear fit R2 0.80; linearising changes AUC by -0.0003; restoring alone adds 0.002. Nearly negligible.
variables: number of calls to customer service

reference_patient.definition: the typical patient: the median training patient for every number and the most common training category for every category (not a real patient)

confidence_rules.clearly: a meaningful change in predicted risk for a typical patient (at least 5% points), the test split agrees (same sign, and its bootstrap interval over test patients excludes no benefit), and every group has at least 20 training patients
confidence_rules.consistently across patients: the claim holds for at least 90% of training patients (range across patients); this is not a significance statement
confidence_rules.on the training data only: the test split disagrees (opposite sign, or no benefit on test patients) or is unclear (its interval includes no benefit), or no test check is available
confidence_rules.slightly: the change in predicted risk for a typical patient is below 5% points
confidence_rules.the model has little data on this: a compared group has fewer than 20 training patients

settings.effect_scale: log-odds (output pre-activation) for verification; predicted risk for the typical patient for wording
